British cheeses.Cheddar: Named for a Somerset village with a famous gorge, it is the most popular cheese in Britain and is now made all over the world.
British cheeses.Stilton: Protected status means true Stilton can only be made in three English counties, yet none of them includes the village of Stilton itself.
British cheeses.Wensleydale: Wallace and Gromit's favourite cheese was nearly lost in 1992, until their film made it so famous that the Yorkshire dairy was saved.
British cheeses.Red Leicester: Its deep orange colour comes from annatto, a plant dye, and it makes a handsome, nutty melt on toast.
British cheeses.Double Gloucester: The 'double' probably refers to its richer, bigger recipe; it is famously chased down Cooper's Hill in an annual wheel-rolling race.
British cheeses.Cheshire: One of Britain's oldest named cheeses, it is even listed in the Domesday Book of 1086, and it has a crumbly, slightly salty bite.
British cheeses.Caerphilly: This crumbly white Welsh cheese was once the packed lunch of local coal miners, who valued how well its saltiness replaced what they sweated out.
British cheeses.Lancashire: Made with curds from different days, the blend gives it a creamy texture, and it is known as the 'Tasty' toasting cheese.
British cheeses.Shropshire Blue: Despite the name, it was created in Scotland in the 1970s; annatto gives it an orange tint that contrasts with its blue veins.
British cheeses.Stinking Bishop: Washed in perry made from a pear variety of the same name, this smelly Gloucestershire cheese was a surprise film star in Wallace and Gromit.
British cheeses.Brie: A soft cheese from the Île-de-France region of France; it is a trap here because it is French, not British.
British cheeses.Gouda: Dutch, not British. It is named after a city in the Netherlands, and aged versions develop crunchy crystals of amino acids.
British cheeses.Edam: Dutch, so it doesn't fit. Its red wax coating once made it ideal for long sea voyages, as it keeps well without refrigeration.
British cheeses.Jarlsberg: A mild Norwegian cheese with big holes, created by a university dairy team in the 1950s from a historic recipe.
British cheeses.Monterey Jack: An American cheese from California, supposedly named after a Monterey dairy owner called David Jacks, so not British.
British cheeses.Colby: An American cheese from Colby, Wisconsin, where it was first made in 1885; it is softer and moister than Cheddar.
British cheeses.Feta: A Greek brined cheese made mostly from sheep's milk; its name is protected in the EU, and Greeks eat more cheese per person than almost anyone.
British cheeses.Halloumi: Cyprus is its home, and it is so firm and heat-resistant that it can be grilled or fried without melting.
British cheeses.Gruyère: Swiss, named after a town in Fribourg; it is the traditional cheese for fondue and French onion soup.
British cheeses.Roquefort: French, not British. This sheep's milk blue cheese must be aged in the natural caves at Roquefort-sur-Soulzon to carry the name.
British cheeses.Havarti: A buttery cheese from Denmark, developed in the 1800s by a farmer's wife called Hanne Nielsen who travelled around Europe to learn cheese-making.
British cheeses.Manchego: Spanish, made only from the milk of Manchega sheep in La Mancha, the region where Don Quixote is set.
British cheeses.Gorgonzola: An Italian blue cheese from Lombardy, said to be named after a village near Milan, and it is often softer and creamier than Stilton.
British cheeses.Emmental: The Swiss cheese with the famous holes, which come from bubbles of gas made by bacteria as the cheese ripens.

French pastries and desserts.Croissant: Its ancestor was the Austrian kipferl, but French bakers perfected the flaky laminated dough with many layers of butter.
French pastries and desserts.Éclair: The name means 'lightning' in French, possibly because you eat it so quickly; the choux pastry is filled with cream and glazed.
French pastries and desserts.Macaron: A delicate almond meringue sandwich; Ladurée in Paris popularised the filled version in the 20th century.
French pastries and desserts.Mille-feuille: The name means 'thousand leaves', for its layers of puff pastry sandwiched with custard cream.
French pastries and desserts.Profiterole: A choux pastry puff filled with cream and doused in chocolate sauce, and often stacked in a tower at weddings.
French pastries and desserts.Madeleine: A shell-shaped sponge cake that triggered Marcel Proust's memories in 'In Search of Lost Time'.
French pastries and desserts.Pain au chocolat: A flaky pastry with chocolate bars inside; in parts of southwest France it is known as a 'chocolatine'.
French pastries and desserts.Crème brûlée: The name means 'burnt cream'; it's a smooth custard topped with caramelised sugar that cracks under a spoon.
French pastries and desserts.Paris-Brest: A ring of choux pastry filled with praline cream, created in 1910 to honour a bicycle race between Paris and Brest.
French pastries and desserts.Canelé: A small Bordeaux cake with a dark, caramelised crust and a soft custard centre, baked in copper moulds.
French pastries and desserts.Religieuse: Two stacked choux buns, one big and one small, said to look like a nun in her habit, hence 'religieuse'.
French pastries and desserts.Financier: A small almond cake, said to be shaped like a gold bar for the stockbrokers of Paris's financial district.
French pastries and desserts.Kouign-amann: A Breton pastry whose name means 'butter cake'; it is a caramelised mix of butter, sugar and dough, and very rich.
French pastries and desserts.Cannoli: A Sicilian pastry shell filled with sweet ricotta, so Italian, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Tiramisu: An Italian dessert whose name means 'pick me up'.
French pastries and desserts.Baklava: Layered filo, nuts and syrup, eaten across Turkey, Greece and the Middle East, not France.
French pastries and desserts.Churro: A Spanish fried dough stick, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Strudel: An Austrian pastry with thin dough rolled around fruit, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Panna cotta: An Italian cooked cream dessert from Piedmont, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Pastel de nata: A Portuguese custard tart, first made by monks in Lisbon, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Brownie: An American chocolate bake, with a chewy, fudgy crumb, and not a French pastry.
French pastries and desserts.Lamington: An Australian cake covered in chocolate and coconut, not French.
French pastries and desserts.Cheesecake: A dessert that dates back to ancient Greece, and not a French pastry in particular.
French pastries and desserts.Sfogliatella: A shell-shaped Italian pastry from Naples, not French.

Rivers of South America.Amazon: Carries more water than the next seven rivers combined, around one fifth of all river water entering the oceans. Its mouth is so wide that you can't see across.
Rivers of South America.Orinoco: One of South America's longest rivers, running through Venezuela and Colombia. A natural channel, the Casiquiare, links it to the Amazon basin.
Rivers of South America.Paraná: This river flows through Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina. Its name means like the sea in Tupi, and Itaipu, a giant dam, is on it.
Rivers of South America.Magdalena: Colombia's main river carries the nation's trade from the Andes to the Caribbean. The name honors Mary Magdalene, and it's heavy with silt.
Rivers of South America.São Francisco: Brazil's longest river that is wholly within the country, flowing through the dry northeast. It is nicknamed the River of National Unity.
Rivers of South America.Uruguay: The river borders Argentina and Uruguay, and lends the country its name. The name likely comes from a Guaraní phrase for river of the painted birds.
Rivers of South America.Paraguay: This river flows through the country of the same name, dividing it into two very different halves, and feeds the huge Pantanal wetlands.
Rivers of South America.Madeira: The Amazon's biggest tributary, named for the floating logs it carries. It's one of the longest tributaries in the world.
Rivers of South America.Rio Negro: The Amazon's blackwater giant is dark with tannins. Where it meets the cloudy Solimões, the two flow side by side for kilometers without mixing.
Rivers of South America.Xingu: A major Amazon tributary in Brazil, home to many Indigenous peoples. The Belo Monte dam on it is one of the world's biggest.
Rivers of South America.Rio Grande: Despite its name, this one is not in South America. It flows from Colorado to the Gulf of Mexico, marking the Texas-Mexico border.
Rivers of South America.Mississippi: This is North America's great river, flowing through the United States into the Gulf of Mexico.
Rivers of South America.Nile: Africa's great river flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean.
Rivers of South America.Congo: Africa's deepest river, with the world's second largest flow, runs through the center of that continent.
Rivers of South America.Mekong: Southeast Asia's great river runs through six countries from Tibet to Vietnam.
Rivers of South America.Yukon: This river flows from Canada through Alaska to the Bering Sea, far to the north.
Rivers of South America.Hudson: New York's river, named for explorer Henry Hudson, is in North America.
Rivers of South America.Danube: Europe's second longest river flows from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea.
Rivers of South America.Ganges: India's sacred river flows into the Bay of Bengal.
Rivers of South America.Niger: West Africa's great river takes a strange boomerang-shaped route, in Africa.
Rivers of South America.Tagus: The longest river on the Iberian Peninsula flows through Spain and Portugal to Lisbon.
Rivers of South America.Ebro: Spain's largest river by flow runs to the Mediterranean, and it's in Europe.
Rivers of South America.Douro: The river flows through Portugal's port wine country, in Europe.
Rivers of South America.Volga: Europe's longest river is in Russia, and flows to the Caspian Sea.

Indigenous languages of the Americas.Quechua: The Inca language, still spoken by millions across the Andes, making it one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages in the Americas.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Navajo: Navajo code talkers used their language to send secret Marine messages in the Pacific in the Second World War, and the code was never broken.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Nahuatl: The language of the Aztecs gave English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado and chili.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Cherokee: Sequoyah invented its writing system, a syllabary, around 1821, mostly by himself, and literacy spread rapidly.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Guarani: Official in Paraguay alongside Spanish, and spoken by most Paraguayans, which is rare for an Indigenous language.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Aymara: Spoken around Lake Titicaca in Bolivia and Peru, with a grammar that puts the past in front of speakers and future behind them.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Inuktitut: An Inuit language of Arctic Canada, official in Nunavut, written in syllabics.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Cree: One of Canada's most widely spoken Indigenous languages, with dialects across the country from Alberta to Quebec.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Lakota: A Siouan language of the Great Plains, and the language of Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Ojibwe: An Algonquian language around the Great Lakes. The Ojibwe also gave us the word totem.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Mohawk: An Iroquoian language of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the Six Nations, and still taught in immersion schools.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Maori: It is the Polynesian language of New Zealand, from the Pacific rather than the Americas.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Sami: The Indigenous languages of northern Scandinavia, spoken by reindeer herders, which are European, not American.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Zulu: A Bantu language of southern Africa, not an American language.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Swahili: An East African lingua franca, with no Indigenous American origin.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Basque: Europe's language isolate, from the Pyrenees, unrelated to any American tongue.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Welsh: A Celtic language of Wales that enjoys revival, and unrelated to Indigenous American languages.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Gaelic: A Celtic language from Scotland and Ireland, though Scottish Gaelic did reach Nova Scotia with settlers.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Tagalog: A language of the Philippines, with many Spanish loanwords, and not an American one.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Ainu: The Indigenous language of northern Japan, with few remaining speakers and no American link.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Tibetan: A language of the Himalayan plateau, written in an Indian-derived script, not an American one.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Berber: The Amazigh languages of North Africa, among the continent's oldest, not American.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Yoruba: A West African language, though its religious traditions travelled to the Americas and survive in Santeria and Candomble.
Indigenous languages of the Americas.Samoan: A Polynesian language of the Pacific, not of the Americas.

Units named after scientists.Newton: Isaac Newton described gravity and the laws of motion, and one newton is about the weight of a small apple.
Units named after scientists.Joule: James Prescott Joule, an English brewer's son, showed that heat and mechanical work are equivalent.
Units named after scientists.Watt: James Watt improved the steam engine in the 1700s, and he also coined the term 'horsepower'.
Units named after scientists.Volt: Alessandro Volta invented the first true battery in 1800, the voltaic pile of stacked metal discs.
Units named after scientists.Ampere: André-Marie Ampère founded electrodynamics, and the ampere honors him.
Units named after scientists.Ohm: Georg Ohm found that current relates to voltage and resistance, a law that was first poorly received.
Units named after scientists.Pascal: Blaise Pascal studied fluids and pressure, and built an early mechanical calculator as a teenager.
Units named after scientists.Hertz: Heinrich Hertz proved radio waves exist in the 1880s, and one hertz is one cycle per second.
Units named after scientists.Kelvin: William Thomson took the title Lord Kelvin from the River Kelvin in Glasgow, and the kelvin begins at absolute zero.
Units named after scientists.Coulomb: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured electric forces in the 1780s, and one coulomb is about 6.24 quintillion electron charges.
Units named after scientists.Tesla: Nikola Tesla gave his name to the unit of magnetic flux density; hospital MRI scanners are rated at 1.5 or 3 teslas.
Units named after scientists.Farad: Michael Faraday's name is on the farad, a huge unit, so most capacitors are measured in microfarads.
Units named after scientists.Henry: Joseph Henry discovered self-induction and became the first Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.
Units named after scientists.Meter: A trap: the meter comes from the Greek metron, 'measure', not from a person.
Units named after scientists.Gram: A trap: the gram isn't a person's name; it derives from a Greek word for a small weight.
Units named after scientists.Second: A trap: the second comes from Latin 'secunda minuta', the second small division of an hour, not a scientist.
Units named after scientists.Liter: A trap: the liter isn't named for a person; it traces to an old French unit, the litron.
Units named after scientists.Mole: A trap: the mole comes from the German word Molekül, not from a scientist.
Units named after scientists.Mile: A trap: the mile comes from the Latin 'mille passus', a thousand paces.
Units named after scientists.Foot: A trap: the foot comes from the human foot, not a scientist.
Units named after scientists.Calorie: A trap: the calorie comes from the Latin 'calor', meaning heat.
Units named after scientists.Acre: A trap: the acre comes from an Old English word for open field, not a person.
Units named after scientists.Ounce: A trap: the ounce comes from Latin 'uncia', a twelfth part.
Units named after scientists.Candela: A trap: the candela is Latin for candle, so it isn't named after a person.

Animals that have been to space.Dog: Laika, a Moscow street dog, orbited Earth in 1957 aboard Sputnik 2. Later dogs like Belka and Strelka returned alive in 1960.
Animals that have been to space.Chimpanzee: Ham flew a suborbital hop in January 1961, months before Alan Shepard. Enos then orbited Earth twice in November 1961.
Animals that have been to space.Monkey: Monkeys flew from the 1940s on, before humans did. Able and Baker survived a 1959 flight in a US Jupiter missile nose cone.
Animals that have been to space.Cat: Félicette, a Paris stray, flew in a French rocket in 1963 and returned alive. She is the only cat known to have reached space.
Animals that have been to space.Mouse: Mice have flown in space many times. Studying them in orbit has helped scientists learn how weightlessness weakens bone and muscle.
Animals that have been to space.Fruit fly: The first animals in space, launched on a US V-2 rocket in 1947. Scientists wanted to study the effect of radiation at altitude.
Animals that have been to space.Tardigrade: These tiny 'water bears' in 2007 survived exposure to open space in a Russian capsule. They can dry out and wait for years.
Animals that have been to space.Tortoise: Two Russian tortoises circled the Moon on Zond 5 in 1968, before any humans did. They came back healthy, though hungry.
Animals that have been to space.Spider: Spiders Arabella and Anita spun webs on Skylab in 1973. Their orbit webs were thinner but still worked.
Animals that have been to space.Jellyfish: Thousands of moon jellyfish went up on the 1991 shuttle flight. Their offspring born in orbit had trouble with gravity back on Earth.
Animals that have been to space.Frog: Frogs have been to space to test how gravity affects development. Tadpoles raised in orbit swam in circles, showing balance changes.
Animals that have been to space.Fish: Medaka fish bred in space on a 1994 shuttle flight, becoming the first vertebrates to mate and produce young in orbit.
Animals that have been to space.Newt: Famous for regrowing lost limbs, newts have flown in orbit so scientists could study how weightlessness affects that regeneration.
Animals that have been to space.Rat: Rats have flown on shuttle missions and Soviet satellites. They helped show the effects of microgravity on bones, muscles and balance.
Animals that have been to space.Elephant: No elephant has gone to space. A full-grown one weighs several tons, far too heavy for any early capsule.
Animals that have been to space.Giraffe: No giraffe has gone to space. Launch weight is costly, and a giraffe's tall build and huge blood pressure would make it a poor choice.
Animals that have been to space.Horse: No horse has flown to space. Horses are far too big for the small capsules of early missions, which carried mice, dogs and monkeys.
Animals that have been to space.Cow: No cow has flown to space. Early spaceflights carried small animals such as dogs, monkeys, mice and insects, since big ones were too heavy.
Animals that have been to space.Penguin: Penguins have never flown to space, and they can't even fly in air. Their wings evolved into flippers for swimming.
Animals that have been to space.Kangaroo: No kangaroo has flown to space. Marsupials never made the cut, since agencies picked animals well studied in labs, like rodents and primates.
Animals that have been to space.Dolphin: No dolphin has been to space. They need water and must surface to breathe, so a capsule would be impossible for them.
Animals that have been to space.Lion: No lion has been to space. Agencies chose small, easily handled animals such as mice, dogs and monkeys, not big predators.
Animals that have been to space.Shark: No shark has been to space. Sharks need seawater, and many must keep swimming to push water over their gills, so orbit would not suit them.
Animals that have been to space.Panda: No giant panda has flown to space. Agencies chose small, well-studied animals, and an adult panda weighs over 100 kg.

Characters in Back to the Future.Marty McFly: Eric Stoltz shot about five weeks as Marty before Michael J. Fox replaced him, so Fox filmed Family Ties by day and this by night.
Characters in Back to the Future.Doc Brown: Dr. Emmett Brown says he invented the flux capacitor after hitting his head on a toilet in 1955.
Characters in Back to the Future.Biff Tannen: Thomas F. Wilson played Biff and his descendants. The name reportedly came from a Universal executive, Ned Tanen.
Characters in Back to the Future.George McFly: Crispin Glover's awkward George wasn't in the sequels, leading to a lawsuit over use of his likeness that changed Hollywood contracts.
Characters in Back to the Future.Lorraine: Marty's mother, Lorraine Baines McFly, who in 1955 develops a crush on her own time-traveling son.
Characters in Back to the Future.Einstein: Doc's dog, named for Albert Einstein, is the first living time traveler, sent one minute into the future.
Characters in Back to the Future.Jennifer Parker: Marty's girlfriend was played by Claudia Wells in the first film and by Elisabeth Shue in the sequels.
Characters in Back to the Future.Mr. Strickland: Hill Valley High's strict principal, who tells Marty that no McFly ever amounted to anything.
Characters in Back to the Future.Griff Tannen: Biff's grandson, leader of a gang that rides hoverboards through 2015 in Part II.
Characters in Back to the Future.Goldie Wilson: The 1955 diner worker who, inspired by Marty's suggestion, decides to run for mayor.
Characters in Back to the Future.Ferris Bueller: A different 1980s teen classic, Matthew Broderick's 1986 film set in Chicago, not Hill Valley.
Characters in Back to the Future.Cameron Frye: Ferris's anxious best friend, whose father's prized Ferrari ends up in a ravine.
Characters in Back to the Future.John Connor: The future leader of the human resistance in the Terminator films, not Hill Valley.
Characters in Back to the Future.Sarah Connor: The Terminator's heroine and John's mother, a waitress turned warrior.
Characters in Back to the Future.Elliott: The boy who befriends E.T. in Spielberg's 1982 film. Spielberg also executive-produced Back to the Future.
Characters in Back to the Future.Sloth: The gentle giant of The Goonies (1985), a Spielberg-story film, but not a Hill Valley resident.
Characters in Back to the Future.Chunk: Goonies' Chunk, the Truffle Shuffle kid, is from Astoria, Oregon, not Hill Valley.
Characters in Back to the Future.Gizmo: The cuddly mogwai in Gremlins (1984), another 1980s hit that Spielberg produced.
Characters in Back to the Future.Ted Logan: One half of Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure, a time-travel comedy, but a different one.
Characters in Back to the Future.Peter Venkman: Bill Murray's Ghostbusters role, a hit of 1984, not a Back to the Future character.
Characters in Back to the Future.Egon Spengler: Ghostbusters' physicist, played by Harold Ramis, who also co-wrote the film.
Characters in Back to the Future.Indiana Jones: Harrison Ford's adventurer, from another Spielberg-era franchise. Not a Back to the Future character.
Characters in Back to the Future.Short Round: Indiana Jones's young sidekick in Temple of Doom (1984).
Characters in Back to the Future.Kevin McCallister: The boy left behind in Home Alone (1990), a different film entirely.

Blue characters from film and TV.Papa Smurf: The cartoon says he is 542 years old and leads the village in a red hat and red trousers, the only Smurf dressed that way.
Blue characters from film and TV.Stitch: Experiment 626 is a blue alien whose film popularized the Hawaiian idea that 'ohana means family, and family means nobody gets left behind.
Blue characters from film and TV.Sulley: Pixar gave Sulley over two million individually animated hairs, a technical feat that made his fur a showpiece in 2001.
Blue characters from film and TV.Cookie Monster: The monster first showed up in 1966 General Foods ads, long before he joined Sesame Street as the cookie lover.
Blue characters from film and TV.Grover: Sesame Street's furry blue monster has a hero alter ego, Super Grover, who often crash-lands and bumbles through rescues.
Blue characters from film and TV.Genie: Robin Williams improvised hours of material for the Genie, and animators drew the character to fit his voice.
Blue characters from film and TV.Dory: A blue tang with short-term memory loss; blue tangs are real reef fish, and the film's popularity pushed sales as pets.
Blue characters from film and TV.Sonic: His blue was chosen to match Sega's logo, as the company wanted a mascot to challenge Mario in 1991.
Blue characters from film and TV.Megamind: DreamWorks' big-headed blue villain turns hero in this 2010 film, with Will Ferrell voicing the title role.
Blue characters from film and TV.Mystique: The X-Men's blue-skinned shapeshifter has been played by Rebecca Romijn and Jennifer Lawrence in different films.
Blue characters from film and TV.Dr. Manhattan: The only true superpowered being in Watchmen is a physicist rebuilt atom by atom after a lab accident, and he glows blue.
Blue characters from film and TV.Sadness: Inside Out's blue emotion is voiced by Phyllis Smith, who also played Phyllis on The Office.
Blue characters from film and TV.Neytiri: Avatar's Na'vi are blue-skinned and about ten feet tall, and Neytiri is the clan leader's daughter and heroine.
Blue characters from film and TV.Elmo: Trap: Elmo is red, not blue, and the Sesame Street monster has been three and a half years old for decades.
Blue characters from film and TV.Shrek: Shrek is green, not blue, and the ogre was based on a character in William Steig's picture book.
Blue characters from film and TV.Kermit: Kermit is green; his song 'Rainbow Connection' earned an Oscar nomination in 1980.
Blue characters from film and TV.Pikachu: Pikachu is yellow with a lightning-bolt tail, and he is Pokemon number 25 in the Pokedex.
Blue characters from film and TV.Garfield: Garfield is orange, a lasagna-loving cat who debuted in Jim Davis's comic strip in 1978.
Blue characters from film and TV.Patrick Star: Patrick Star is pink and lives under a rock in Bikini Bottom, next door to SpongeBob.
Blue characters from film and TV.Big Bird: Big Bird is yellow and stands about eight feet tall; Caroll Spinney performed him for nearly fifty years.
Blue characters from film and TV.Barney: Barney is purple, a T. rex who became a PBS preschool sensation in the early 1990s.
Blue characters from film and TV.Hulk: The Hulk is green, though in his first 1962 comic he was gray before Marvel changed his color.
Blue characters from film and TV.Mike Wazowski: Mike Wazowski is green and one-eyed, and often mistaken for blue when standing next to his best friend Sulley.
Blue characters from film and TV.Pink Panther: The Pink Panther is pink from head to toe, and he began as a cartoon in the 1963 film's opening titles.

Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Porky Pig: Porky wears a jacket and bow tie but no pants, and Mel Blanc voiced his stutter.
Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Yogi Bear: Yogi wears a hat, collar and tie, and no pants; he claims to be smarter than the average bear.
Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Scrooge McDuck: Scrooge wears a top hat, spats and coat, and no trousers; Carl Barks created him in 1947.

Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Bugs Bunny: Bugs wears gloves but never pants; he officially debuted in 1940's A Wild Hare.
Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Scooby-Doo: Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane in only a collar, and he first appeared in 1969.

Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Huey: Huey wears a hat and shirt like his triplet brothers, Dewey and Louie, but no pants.

Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.SpongeBob: SpongeBob's pants are right in his name, brown square ones that are rarely off.

Cartoon characters who don't wear pants.Dora: Dora wears a pink shirt and orange shorts, so she is not pantless.

Adele songs.Hello: Her 2015 comeback single was the first song to sell over a million downloads in a week in the US.
Adele songs.Someone Like You: A quiet piano ballad from 21, whose live performance at the 2011 Brit Awards sent it to number one.
Adele songs.Rolling in the Deep: The lead single from 21, it was a worldwide hit and won her Grammys for Record of the Year in 2012.
Adele songs.Skyfall: The 2012 James Bond theme won the Oscar for Best Original Song, the first Bond theme to do so.
Adele songs.Set Fire to the Rain: A pop-soul hit from 21 with a stormy chorus, and it gave her a Grammy-winning live version recorded at the Royal Albert Hall.
Adele songs.Easy on Me: The lead single from 30, released in 2021, was about her divorce and broke streaming records on its first day.
Adele songs.Chasing Pavements: Her breakout 2008 single was nominated for a Grammy for Record of the Year and made her a star in the UK.
Adele songs.When We Were Young: A powerful ballad from 25, and the song's live performance for a TV special in 2015 became one of her most-viewed videos.

Things that hiss.Snake: Snakes lack vocal cords; the hiss is just air forced out through the glottis, often as a warning.
Things that hiss.Angry cat: Some biologists think a cat's hiss imitates a snake, a bluff that startles predators.
Things that hiss.Goose: A goose hisses with its neck stretched low to warn intruders; Roman legend says sacred geese saved the Capitol.
Things that hiss.Swan: A mute swan hisses and snorts, so the name 'mute' is a bit misleading.
Things that hiss.Leaky tire: Car tires hold around 32 psi, so a hiss means that pressure is escaping.
Things that hiss.Opened soda: Dissolved carbon dioxide escapes when you pop the top; Joseph Priestley invented carbonated water in 1767.
Things that hiss.TV static: A little of the fuzz on old analog TVs was leftover radiation from the Big Bang, a small share of the noise.
Things that hiss.Possum: Opossums hiss, showing 50 teeth, more than any other land mammal in North America.
Things that hiss.Espresso machine: The steam wand hisses, and espresso is brewed at about nine bars of pressure.
Things that hiss.Dog: Dogs bark, growl and whine; they also pant, but none of those is a hiss, and a hissing dog would be a rare sound.
Things that hiss.Lion: A lion's roar can carry about eight kilometers, a booming sound that is the opposite of a hiss.
Things that hiss.Cow: Cows moo, and studies suggest they form close friendships and get stressed when separated from them; a hiss isn't in their vocabulary.
Things that hiss.Pig: Pigs grunt and squeal rather than hiss, and they are often ranked among the smartest farm animals.
Things that hiss.Trumpet: A trumpet blasts, a brassy sound produced by buzzing lips into a mouthpiece; no hissing there.
Things that hiss.Snare drum: Snare wires buzz and crack against the drum head; jazz brushes make a soft swish, but not a true hiss.
Things that hiss.Doorbell: A doorbell chimes ding-dong when plungers strike two metal tone bars; hissing is a different, airy sound.
Things that hiss.Sheep: Sheep bleat, and research suggests they can recognize dozens of other sheep faces, but they don't hiss.
Things that hiss.Horse: Horses neigh, whinny and snort, and can doze while standing thanks to a locking joint in their legs.
Things that hiss.Church bell: A church bell tolls or peals, a ringing metallic note that is the opposite of a hiss.
Things that hiss.Rooster: Roosters crow on a body clock, so they do it even in the dark; hissing isn't part of the show.
Things that hiss.Frog: Frogs croak and ribbit, with sound made by air passing over vocal cords and amplified by a throat sac.
Things that hiss.Donkey: Donkeys bray, a loud hee-haw that can carry for miles in open country, rather than hiss.
Things that hiss.Bee: Bees buzz because their wings beat roughly 230 times a second; it's a hum, not a hiss.
Things that hiss.Tuba: Tubas boom; a big one holds about 18 feet of coiled tubing, and the sound is deep, not airy.

Sports with a goalkeeper.Water polo: The goalkeeper treads water, usually with an eggbeater kick, while defending a goal almost 3 meters wide.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Lacrosse: The goalie's crosse has a wider head, and blocks shots that can travel over 100 mph.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Hurling: An Irish stick-and-ball sport, thousands of years old, whose goalkeeper defends a goal with a net below the crossbar.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Gaelic football: Another Irish game; the goalkeeper is allowed to handle the ball within the small rectangle, and goals are worth three points.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Futsal: A five-a-side indoor soccer game, with a smaller heavier ball, where goalkeepers are often joined by an outfield-playing keeper.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Bandy: Played on a field of ice with a ball, with 11 players per side, and sometimes called 'Russian hockey'.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Floorball: A fast indoor hockey sport using a plastic stick and hole-filled ball, where goalies play without sticks.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Basketball: The goal is a hoop above the court, which is not defended by a designated goalie; goaltending is a violation.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Volleyball: Played over a net, with no goalkeeper, but the libero is a defensive specialist in a different shirt.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Rugby: There's no goalkeeper; the posts are guarded by the full-back and others who can use hands everywhere.
Sports with a goalkeeper.American football: There's no goalie, because defenders try to stop a ball carrier, not a shot, across the end zone.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Baseball: Baseball has a catcher and a pitcher, but no goalie, since the goal is to hit and run.
Sports with a goalkeeper.Cricket: The wicketkeeper stands behind the stumps, but their job is catching, not blocking a goal.

Creatures from Norse myth.Fenrir: The monstrous wolf son of Loki was bound by the gods with a magic ribbon, and is fated to kill Odin at Ragnarok.
Creatures from Norse myth.Jormungandr: The Midgard Serpent grew so long it encircles the world and bites its own tail; Thor is fated to kill it, and die of its venom.
Creatures from Norse myth.Sleipnir: Odin's eight-legged horse was the child of Loki, in mare form, and the stallion Svadilfari.
Creatures from Norse myth.Nidhogg: A dragon gnawing the roots of the world tree Yggdrasil, he also feeds on the bodies of the dead.
Creatures from Norse myth.Ratatoskr: A squirrel that runs up and down Yggdrasil carrying insults between the eagle above and Nidhogg below.
Creatures from Norse myth.Valkyrie: Odin's battle maidens choose which warriors die and take them to Valhalla; Wagner made the name famous.
Creatures from Norse myth.Draugr: Norse sagas describe these undead guarding their grave goods, and they were stronger and heavier than the living.
Creatures from Norse myth.Huginn: One of Odin's two ravens, its name means 'thought'; each morning it flies across the world to bring news back.
Creatures from Norse myth.Muninn: Odin's raven of 'memory'; he worried more about Muninn not returning than Huginn, since memory is harder to replace.
Creatures from Norse myth.Hati: This wolf chases the moon across the sky, and at Ragnarok is fated to catch and swallow it.
Creatures from Norse myth.Skoll: A wolf who hunts the sun through the sky; his name suggests 'treachery', and eclipses were once blamed on him.
Creatures from Norse myth.Garm: The blood-stained hound guarding Hel's gates; he'll fight the god Tyr at Ragnarok, each killing the other.
Creatures from Norse myth.Pegasus: A trap: this winged horse is Greek, not Norse; Odin rode the eight-legged Sleipnir.
Creatures from Norse myth.Cerberus: A trap: the three-headed hound of Hades is Greek; Norse myth has Garm guarding Hel's gate.
Creatures from Norse myth.Minotaur: A trap: the bull-headed monster belongs to Crete and Greek myth, far from the Norse world.
Creatures from Norse myth.Hydra: Heracles killed this many-headed Greek water serpent; each severed head grew back as two.
Creatures from Norse myth.Phoenix: A trap: the firebird reborn from ashes is Greek-Egyptian, with no Norse counterpart.
Creatures from Norse myth.Sphinx: Greek and Egyptian, the lion-bodied riddler of Thebes; nothing like it appears in Norse myth.
Creatures from Norse myth.Griffin: Eagle-lion hybrids are Persian and Greek; Norse tales favor wolves, ravens and serpents.
Creatures from Norse myth.Unicorn: A trap: the one-horned horse comes from Greek writers and medieval Europe, not Norse sagas.
Creatures from Norse myth.Chimera: A fire-breathing Greek monster with lion, goat and snake parts, and not a Norse myth.
Creatures from Norse myth.Ammit: An Egyptian devourer of hearts, part crocodile, lion and hippo, who ate the unworthy in the afterlife.
Creatures from Norse myth.Kitsune: A trap: Japanese fox spirits grow more tails with age, up to nine; they're not Norse.
Creatures from Norse myth.Basilisk: A medieval European serpent whose gaze could kill, not a creature of the Norse sagas.

Types of saw.Hacksaw: A hacksaw has a thin blade stretched across a frame, and it is built to cut metal and plastic.
Types of saw.Jigsaw: Jigsaw puzzles were named for the saw used to cut them, since early ones were cut from wood by a fine blade.
Types of saw.Circular saw: A circular saw is a spinning toothed disc, and a handheld one can cut through lumber in seconds.
Types of saw.Chainsaw: The chainsaw was reportedly first designed for childbirth in the 1780s, to help surgeons cut bone and cartilage.
Types of saw.Bandsaw: A bandsaw has a continuous loop of toothed blade, making it great for cutting curves and resawing lumber.
Types of saw.Coping saw: A coping saw has a thin blade in a deep frame, designed for cutting tight curves, such as joints in molding.
Types of saw.Table saw: A table saw has a blade rising through a flat table, and it is the workhorse of many woodworking shops.
Types of saw.Miter saw: A miter saw pivots to cut precise angles, which is how picture frames get their neat corners.
Types of saw.Bow saw: A bow saw has a tubular frame and a blade kept tight like a bowstring, and it is popular for trimming branches.
Types of saw.Handsaw: A handsaw's teeth are angled to cut on the push or pull stroke, and handsaws date back to ancient Egypt.
Types of saw.Scroll saw: A scroll saw has a thin blade moving up and down, ideal for intricate fretwork and puzzle shapes.
Types of saw.Seesaw: A seesaw is a playground teeter-totter, and its name imitates the back-and-forth motion of sawing.
Types of saw.Chisel: A chisel shaves or carves by pushing or tapping, and it cuts by wedging, not by teeth.
Types of saw.Drill: A drill bores holes with a spinning bit, rather than cutting a line with teeth.
Types of saw.Hand plane: A hand plane shaves thin curls off wood with a sharp blade, smoothing the surface.
Types of saw.Router: A woodworking router spins a bit at high speed to hollow out grooves and shape edges.
Types of saw.Sander: A sander smooths surfaces with abrasive paper, and it grinds away rather than cutting with teeth.
Types of saw.Rasp: A rasp is a coarse file for shaping wood, with raised points instead of saw teeth.
Types of saw.Axe: An axe splits wood with a heavy wedge-shaped blade, not with teeth.
Types of saw.Machete: A machete is a broad blade for chopping vegetation, with a plain edge instead of teeth.
Types of saw.Scissors: Scissors are two blades that pivot together, and they cut with a shearing action rather than saw teeth.
Types of saw.Lathe: A lathe spins the wood while a fixed tool shapes it, so the material moves, not the blade.
Types of saw.Hatchet: A hatchet is a small one-handed axe, and its plain edge chops rather than saws.
Types of saw.Utility knife: A utility knife has a retractable blade with a smooth edge, so it slices instead of sawing.

Things that have a tongue.Bell: A bell's tongue is its clapper, the weight inside that strikes the bell, which swings to make the sound.
Things that have a tongue.Dog: A dog's tongue cools it down: dogs have few sweat glands, so panting evaporates water from the tongue to lose heat.
Things that have a tongue.Frog: A frog can flick out its sticky tongue in a fraction of a second, and its tongue is attached at the front of the mouth.
Things that have a tongue.Snake: A snake flicks its forked tongue to collect scent particles, which it passes into an organ on the roof of its mouth.
Things that have a tongue.Giraffe: A giraffe's tongue is about 18 inches long and dark purple, and it's thought to protect it from sunburn while eating.
Things that have a tongue.Chameleon: A chameleon's tongue can be up to twice its body length, and it shoots out in a fraction of a second to catch insects.
Things that have a tongue.Oxford shoe: Oxford shoes have a tongue hidden under closed laces, and the style was named for Oxford University students in the 1800s.
Things that have a tongue.Cat: A cat's tongue is covered with tiny hooked barbs called papillae, which work like a hairbrush when grooming.
Things that have a tongue.Hummingbird: A hummingbird laps up nectar with a forked tongue that acts as a pump, flicking in and out about 13 times a second.
Things that have a tongue.Anteater: A giant anteater's tongue can reach around 2 feet long and flick in and out about 150 times a minute to gather ants.
Things that have a tongue.Sock: A sock has no tongue, though it does have a heel and a toe; this trap is for a clothing item that does not.
Things that have a tongue.Flip-flop: Flip-flops have a thong strap between the toes, and the thong is not a tongue, though the two sound alike.
Things that have a tongue.Hat: A hat has a brim and a crown, but no tongue; a baseball cap, though, has a 'bill' at its front.
Things that have a tongue.Glove: A glove has fingers, thumb, and a cuff, but no tongue, even though a few types of mitts have a wrist closure.
Things that have a tongue.Jellyfish: A jellyfish has no brain, heart, or tongue; it's about 95 percent water and has a simple mouth in the middle.
Things that have a tongue.Starfish: A starfish has no tongue; it pushes its stomach out of its mouth to digest food outside its body.
Things that have a tongue.Mitten: A mitten has a thumb section but no tongue, and the name goes back to a French word for 'half-glove'.
Things that have a tongue.Belt: A belt's buckle has a metal prong, but players know the tongue-of-a-shoe sense; a belt itself has no tongue in that way, so it's a trap.
Things that have a tongue.Scarf: A scarf has no tongue, and it dates back to ancient Rome, where soldiers wore cloth to keep their necks clean.
Things that have a tongue.Worm: An earthworm has no tongue; it breathes through its skin and has no lungs, which is why it surfaces in heavy rain.
Things that have a tongue.Sponge: A sponge is an animal with no tongue, no mouth, and no organs, and it filters food from water that flows through.
Things that have a tongue.Necktie: A necktie has a wide end and a narrow end, but no tongue, and the style came from Croatian soldiers in the 1600s.

Kitchen gadgets you turn or crank.Whisk: A whisk works by hand motion, not turning, and its wire loops add air to eggs and cream.

Kitchen gadgets you turn or crank.Pizza cutter: A pizza cutter has a wheel that rolls along, but you push it and don't crank it.
Kitchen gadgets you turn or crank.Pastry brush: A pastry brush is for painting glaze onto dough and has nothing to turn.

Things you can grate.Cheese: Cheese is the classic grating job. A cold, firm block grates cleanly, while soft cheese just clumps.
Things you can grate.Carrot: Grated carrot sweetens cakes, and its natural sugars and moisture are why carrot cake stays so tender.
Things you can grate.Nutmeg: Whole nutmeg is the seed of a tropical tree. It grates into a fragrant spice far stronger than the pre-ground type.
Things you can grate.Ginger: Frozen ginger is far easier to grate, and the stringy fibers stay behind on the grater instead of clumping.
Things you can grate.Lemon zest: Zest is the colored outer rind. The white pith below it is bitter, so graters should only skim the surface.
Things you can grate.Chocolate: Grated chocolate makes pretty curls for desserts, though it works best when the bar is cold.
Things you can grate.Potato: Grated potato makes rosti and latkes. Squeezing out the water is the secret to crispy edges.
Things you can grate.Garlic: Grating garlic on a fine grater releases juice and flavor, giving a paste ready for dressings.
Things you can grate.Zucchini: Zucchini is about 95 percent water, so grated zucchini should be squeezed dry before it goes into bread or fritters.
Things you can grate.Apple: Grated apple melts into oatmeal and cakes, adding sweetness and moisture while its pectin helps hold things together.
Things you can grate.Cucumber: Grated cucumber is the base of tzatziki and raita, though the water must be squeezed out first.
Things you can grate.Cold butter: Grating cold butter into flour is a pastry trick: the tiny cold shreds stay solid and make the crust flaky.
Things you can grate.Soup: Soup is a liquid, so it just runs through the holes of a grater. You'd need to freeze it first, and that's still a stretch.
Things you can grate.Milk: Milk is a liquid and can't be grated. Frozen milk is a block but would crumble to snow.
Things you can grate.Egg yolk: An egg yolk is soft and runny when raw. Once hard-boiled, though, a yolk will crumble over salads like fine cheese.
Things you can grate.Honey: Honey is too sticky and liquid. Even crystallized honey is better scraped than grated.
Things you can grate.Jelly: Jelly is a wobbly gel that would squish through the holes in a grater, not shred.
Things you can grate.Yogurt: Yogurt is spoonable, not grateable. Strained yogurt can get thick like cheese, though.
Things you can grate.Rice: Rice is already in small grains, so there is nothing to grate. Rice is, however, ground into flour.
Things you can grate.Peas: Peas are small and round and just roll away. They'd get mashed, not shredded.
Things you can grate.Grapes: Grapes would burst into pulp on a grater. They are a classic fruit for squishing, though.
Things you can grate.Olive oil: Olive oil is a liquid, so grating isn't possible. But when chilled hard enough, it solidifies into a waxy paste.
Things you can grate.Ketchup: Ketchup is a thick sauce that just smears across a grater, with nothing to shred.
Things you can grate.Ice cream: Ice cream is far too soft to grate unless frozen rock-hard, and even then it melts on contact with a warm grater.

Illnesses that spread person to person.Flu: Influenza viruses mutate so often that vaccines are reshaped every year, and the 1918 pandemic killed tens of millions.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Common cold: Over 200 viruses can cause colds, with rhinoviruses the main culprits, which is why no single vaccine exists.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Chickenpox: After chickenpox heals, the virus hides in your nerves for life and can return decades later as shingles.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Measles: Measles is among the most contagious diseases known: one case can infect about 12 to 18 unvaccinated people nearby.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Strep throat: Caused by Streptococcus bacteria and treated with antibiotics, it's worth treating to avoid complications like rheumatic fever.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Mumps: The mumps virus swells the salivary glands, giving the classic chipmunk cheeks, and the MMR vaccine prevents it.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Head lice: Lice can't hop or fly; they crawl, so they spread mostly through direct head-to-head contact, not through pets.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Whooping cough: Its name comes from the whoop sound of gasping after a coughing fit, and boosters protect babies who are too young for vaccines.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Norovirus: Norovirus causes cruise-ship stomach outbreaks, and just a few viral particles can make a person sick.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Ringworm: A trap: ringworm has no worm at all. It's a fungal skin infection named for its circular red rash.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Athlete's foot: This fungus thrives in warm damp places like locker room floors, which is how it spreads between people.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Tuberculosis: TB bacteria spread through the air and still infect millions each year, though it's often curable with months of antibiotics.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Diabetes: Diabetes is a metabolic disease that you can't catch, even though type 2 can run in families.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Asthma: Asthma flares from triggers like allergens and exercise, but nobody catches it from another person.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Migraine: A migraine is a neurological condition, not an infection, and it can bring light sensitivity and nausea.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Arthritis: Arthritis is joint inflammation, not an infection, and it affects people of all ages, even children.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Sunburn: Sunburn is skin damage from UV rays, and you can't pass it on, though it raises your skin cancer risk.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Appendicitis: An inflamed appendix isn't contagious, and surgeons have been removing appendixes since the 1880s.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Tetanus: You get tetanus from bacteria in soil entering wounds, not from other people, which is why boosters are given.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Lyme disease: Lyme comes from tick bites, named after Lyme, Connecticut, and it doesn't pass between people in normal contact.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Scurvy: Scurvy comes from lacking vitamin C, which once killed many sailors, and it is cured by oranges, not isolation.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Gout: Gout is a painful buildup of uric acid crystals in joints, often the big toe, and isn't catching.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Acne: Acne is caused by clogged pores and hormones, and it can't be caught from another person's skin.
Illnesses that spread person to person.Hiccups: Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm, and the longest recorded bout lasted about 68 years.

Things that have rings.Saturn: Saturn's rings are mainly chunks of water ice, spanning about 280,000 kilometers across but often only about ten meters thick.
Things that have rings.Uranus: Uranus has faint rings, discovered in 1977, and it orbits tilted on its side, like a rolling ball.
Things that have rings.Neptune: Neptune has faint dark rings, found by Voyager 2 in 1989, and they are partly clumped into bright arcs.
Things that have rings.Jupiter: Jupiter has a thin ring system found by Voyager 1 in 1979, and it is made mostly of dust kicked up from its small moons.
Things that have rings.Tree trunk: Each ring on a cut trunk marks a year of growth, with wide rings in wet years and narrow ones in drought.
Things that have rings.Onion: An onion is made of concentric layers, and cutting one releases a gas that reacts with tear fluid to sting your eyes.
Things that have rings.Olympic flag: The five interlocking rings stand for five regions of the world joined by sport, and designer Pierre de Coubertin drew them in 1913.
Things that have rings.Audi logo: The four interlocking rings of Audi stand for four car companies, Audi, DKW, Horch, and Wanderer, that merged in 1932 as Auto Union.
Things that have rings.Bullseye: A bullseye is the center of a target made of concentric rings, and the word dates to the 1600s.
Things that have rings.Mars: Mars has no rings now, but its moon Phobos is slowly spiraling inward and may break apart into a ring in tens of millions of years.
Things that have rings.Venus: Venus has no rings and no moons, and it spins backward so slowly that one day there is longer than its year.
Things that have rings.Mercury: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and has no rings or moons, and its day lasts about 59 Earth days.
Things that have rings.Earth: Earth has no rings; its moon is large enough to keep orbiting as one body, so no debris ring formed around us.
Things that have rings.The Moon: The Moon has no rings, though a halo can circle it when high ice crystals in our air bend its light.
Things that have rings.The Sun: The Sun has no rings of its own, though ice crystals in Earth's air can produce a glowing circular halo around it.
Things that have rings.Pluto: Pluto has no rings, though a few small worlds do, including the dwarf planet Haumea and the tiny centaur Chariklo.
Things that have rings.Banana: A banana is a smooth curved fruit with no rings, though its peel can show faint ridged lines along its length.
Things that have rings.Carrot: A carrot is a long taproot and not ring-shaped, though a sliced one shows a pale core surrounded by an outer ring.
Things that have rings.Apple logo: Apple's bitten-apple logo has no rings; the first Apple logo in 1976 actually showed Isaac Newton sitting under a tree.
Things that have rings.Nike logo: Nike's Swoosh has no rings; student Carolyn Davidson designed it in 1971 and was paid just 35 dollars for it.
Things that have rings.Pencil: A pencil is a long wooden stick with a graphite core, plus a metal band that holds the eraser, but no rings.
Things that have rings.Brick: A brick is a solid rectangular block, so it has no rings, though it often has holes through it.
Things that have rings.Comet: A comet is a ball of ice and dust that grows a glowing coma and tail near the Sun, but never rings.
Things that have rings.Starfish: A starfish has five arms, usually, but no rings, and many can regrow lost arms, with a few able to regrow a whole body from one.

Things that can give you brain freeze.Ice cream: Brain freeze happens when something cold hits the roof of your mouth and the blood vessels react; the brain itself isn't frozen.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Slushie: A slushie's fine ice crystals chill the palate fast, so a big gulp can cause brain freeze within seconds.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Milkshake: Milkshakes are thick, so sipping slowly helps; a big slurp of a cold one can trigger the same pain.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Popsicle: Popsicles pressed to the roof of your mouth can cause brain freeze; scientists call it sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Frozen yogurt: Frozen yogurt is cold enough to cause brain freeze when eaten fast; the pain peaks after about 30 seconds.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Snow cone: Crushed ice in a snow cone melts slowly and keeps the palate cold, making it a prime brain freeze culprit.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Gelato: Gelato is served a bit warmer than ice cream, so it's gentler, but a big spoonful against the palate can still do it.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Sorbet: Sorbet is cold and dairy-free, so it can still trigger brain freeze if you eat it fast.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Frozen smoothie: Frozen smoothies are cold, thick and drunk through a straw, which can aim the chill at the palate.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Shaved ice: Shaved ice is a fluffy treat from Hawaii, and its cold hits quickly, so brain freeze comes easily.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Hot cocoa: Hot cocoa is a trap: it's the warmest of drinks, so it can't cause brain freeze, which needs sudden cold at the palate.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Soup: Soup is hot, so it risks a scalded tongue, not brain freeze; the pain needs sudden cold on the roof of the mouth.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Coffee: Hot coffee won't cause brain freeze, though an iced coffee gulped fast might; heat brings burns, not that headache.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Tea: Hot tea is the opposite of a brain-freeze trigger; iced tea gulped quickly could, but a steaming cup won't.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Toast: Toast is warm and dry, so there's nothing cold to jolt the palate; it can scrape the roof of your mouth, though.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Pizza: A fresh pizza's cheese can burn the roof of your mouth, but burns are heat damage, not the cold-triggered brain freeze.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Hot dog: Hot dogs are served hot, and the 'brain freeze' needs cold; the biggest risk here is a burnt tongue.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Oatmeal: Oatmeal is served steaming; the cold nerve reaction behind brain freeze can't be set off by hot porridge.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Lasagna: Fresh lasagna is nearly as hot as the oven, so it can't trigger a cold headache; the burn is the real risk.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Ramen: Ramen is served boiling hot, and slurping noodles cools them, but never enough to cause brain freeze.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Pancakes: Pancakes are served warm, so there's no cold stimulus, though ice cream on top would be another story.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Warm milk: Warm milk won't cause brain freeze; the reaction only happens when something cold touches the palate.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Chili: Chili is hot in two ways, temperature and capsaicin; neither creates the cold shock behind brain freeze.
Things that can give you brain freeze.Baked potato: A baked potato comes out of the oven at above 90 C, so no brain freeze, but plenty of steam to burn your tongue.

Things that come out at night.Bats: Most bats hunt at night with echolocation, and a single little brown bat can eat hundreds of mosquito-sized insects in an hour.
Things that come out at night.Owls: Many owls hunt at night, and their feathers have soft edges so they fly almost silently.
Things that come out at night.Moon: The Moon itself doesn't shine; it only reflects sunlight, and it reflects only about 12 percent of what falls on it.
Things that come out at night.Stars: Stars are there during the day, too; the Sun's glare simply hides them.
Things that come out at night.Raccoons: Raccoons are mostly nocturnal, and their sensitive front paws have thousands of nerve endings that help them feel for food.
Things that come out at night.Fireflies: Fireflies make light through a chemical reaction that wastes almost no heat, so their glow is called cold light.
Things that come out at night.Moths: Most moths fly at night, and many use moonlight to navigate, which is why artificial lights confuse them.
Things that come out at night.Hedgehogs: Hedgehogs wander several kilometres a night in search of insects, and they have about 5,000 to 7,000 spines.
Things that come out at night.Vampires: Vampires in legend can't stand sunlight, but that's a modern film idea: Bram Stoker's Dracula walked about in daylight.
Things that come out at night.Werewolves: Werewolves are said to transform under a full moon, a legend that goes back to ancient Greece and Rome.
Things that come out at night.Opossums: Opossums are North America's only marsupial, and they're nocturnal; their famous 'playing dead' is an involuntary response.
Things that come out at night.Crickets: Male crickets chirp by rubbing their wings together, and you can estimate the temperature by counting the chirps.
Things that come out at night.Sun: A trap: the Sun belongs to the day. It's a star about 109 Earths wide, and it's the reason the Moon shines at night.
Things that come out at night.Rooster: Roosters crow at dawn and at other times, thanks to an internal body clock, but they sleep at night.
Things that come out at night.Butterfly: Butterflies are mostly day fliers; they need warmth from the sun to power their flight muscles.
Things that come out at night.Bee: Bees are daytime foragers, and they sleep at night inside the hive, with some staying put on flowers.
Things that come out at night.Squirrel: Squirrels are active by day, and they bury so many nuts that forgotten ones help grow new forests.
Things that come out at night.Rainbow: A rainbow needs sunlight and raindrops, so it's a daytime event, though a rare 'moonbow' can appear at night.
Things that come out at night.Hummingbird: Hummingbirds feed by day, and at night they enter a state called torpor, slowing their heart rate to save energy.
Things that come out at night.Eagle: Eagles hunt by day, and they can spot a rabbit from more than 3 kilometres away.
Things that come out at night.Ladybug: Ladybugs are active by day, and in autumn they gather in groups, sometimes thousands strong, to overwinter together.
Things that come out at night.Pigeon: Pigeons are daytime birds that find their way home using the Sun and Earth's magnetic field.
Things that come out at night.Sunflower: Sunflowers follow the Sun by day while young, then fix facing east; they're a daytime plant, not a night one.
Things that come out at night.Chipmunk: Chipmunks are active in the day, and they store food in underground burrows for winter, hibernating in cold areas.

Things a baker uses.Rolling pin: French pins are tapered with no handles, so the baker can feel the dough's thickness through the palms.
Things a baker uses.Oven: Professional bakery ovens inject steam so that crusts turn shiny and crackly.
Things a baker uses.Mixing bowl: Copper bowls are favored for egg whites, because copper ions help stabilize the foam.
Things a baker uses.Whisk: A balloon whisk's wires beat air into cream and egg whites, multiplying their volume.
Things a baker uses.Proofing basket: Called a banneton, it leaves sourdough loaves with a pattern of flour rings.
Things a baker uses.Piping bag: Different tips pipe roses, stars and shells, turning one bag of icing into dozens of designs.
Things a baker uses.Baking sheet: Pale aluminum sheets bake more evenly than dark ones, which absorb heat and can burn the bottoms.
Things a baker uses.Dough scraper: A bench scraper divides dough into portions and cleans the work surface.
Things a baker uses.Flour sifter: Sifting adds air and breaks lumps, and it also blends dry ingredients evenly.
Things a baker uses.Cooling rack: Air flowing underneath prevents a soggy bottom, and bread continues to set as it cools.
Things a baker uses.Stand mixer: KitchenAid launched its first home stand mixer in 1919, a design that became a kitchen icon.
Things a baker uses.Pastry brush: It spreads egg wash, which gives pastry its glossy golden shine.
Things a baker uses.Trowel: A bricklayer's tool, though a baker's palette knife looks similar and spreads icing.
Things a baker uses.Chisel: A woodworker's tool; Michelangelo famously carved with them.
Things a baker uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's heavy block used for shaping hot metal.
Things a baker uses.Hacksaw: It cuts metal, not dough, and its blades are held in tension.
Things a baker uses.Stethoscope: It listens to the body, and a baker listens to the loaf's crust crackling instead.
Things a baker uses.Plunger: A plumber's suction cup, not a baker's tool.
Things a baker uses.Easel: An artist's stand, and the name comes from the Dutch word for donkey.
Things a baker uses.Pitchfork: A hay fork with long tines, while bakers prick dough with a tiny docking tool.
Things a baker uses.Sickle: A harvest tool for cutting grain, which a baker later turns into flour.
Things a baker uses.Wrench: Used to turn nuts and bolts, and called a spanner in Britain.
Things a baker uses.Gavel: A mallet for judges and auctioneers, not for dough.
Things a baker uses.Kiln: A kiln fires clay at over 1,000 degrees Celsius, while a baker's oven tops out near 250.

Places you'd find a cashier.Supermarket: The first self-service store, Piggly Wiggly, opened in Memphis in 1916, letting shoppers pick goods before paying.
Places you'd find a cashier.Gas station: Many shoppers pay the cashier inside, and prepaying also prevents drive-offs.
Places you'd find a cashier.Pharmacy: A cashier rings up purchases, but a pharmacist must always check prescriptions.
Places you'd find a cashier.Cinema: Box office cashiers sell tickets, but theaters earn most of their profit from the concession stand.
Places you'd find a cashier.Bookstore: Every book carries an ISBN barcode, so one beep identifies any of millions of titles.
Places you'd find a cashier.Department store: John Wanamaker's Philadelphia store helped pioneer fixed price tags, ending haggling.
Places you'd find a cashier.Convenience store: The first 7-Eleven got its name from its original open hours, 7 a.m. to 11 p.m.
Places you'd find a cashier.Fast-food restaurant: McDonald's 1948 Speedee Service System put order and payment at the counter, a model the industry copied.
Places you'd find a cashier.Toy store: Many toy stores make a large share of their yearly sales in the holiday season.
Places you'd find a cashier.Garden center: Cashiers here are busiest in spring, when planting season brings most of the year's trade.
Places you'd find a cashier.Operating room: Surgeons and nurses work here, and no money changes hands at the table.
Places you'd find a cashier.Courtroom: Judges, clerks and lawyers fill it, but fines are paid at a separate office.
Places you'd find a cashier.Classroom: School cafeterias have cashiers, but the classroom does not.
Places you'd find a cashier.Lighthouse: Its keeper tends the light, though some historic lighthouses now have gift shops.
Places you'd find a cashier.Space station: There is no shop aboard the ISS, and astronauts get supplies by cargo ship.
Places you'd find a cashier.Submarine: A sub's crew eats from the galley with no payments, and the vessel is usually a closed community.
Places you'd find a cashier.Ambulance: Paramedics provide care here, and billing happens later at an office.
Places you'd find a cashier.Cockpit: Pilots fly the plane, while cabin crew sell duty-free goods, not the cockpit.
Places you'd find a cashier.Coal mine: Miners dig underground, though company stores above ground once sold them goods.
Places you'd find a cashier.Igloo: An Inuit snow shelter built from blocks of packed snow, with nobody selling anything inside.
Places you'd find a cashier.Fire station: Firefighters wait for calls here, and the building has no checkout counter.
Places you'd find a cashier.Jury room: Jurors deliberate in private, and handling money is not part of the job.
Places you'd find a cashier.Oil rig: Offshore rigs house crews for weeks, but there is no checkout on the platform.
Places you'd find a cashier.Prison cell: Inmates buy snacks through a prison commissary, not at a cashier in their cell.

Search engines.Google: The name derives from googol, 1 followed by 100 zeros, and the company began as a Stanford research project in 1996.
Search engines.Bing: Microsoft launched Bing in 2009 as a successor to its earlier search products, and it powers some other engines too.
Search engines.Yahoo: It began as a hand-built directory of websites in 1994, and became one of the biggest sites of the 1990s.
Search engines.DuckDuckGo: It promises not to track searches, and was founded in 2008 and named after a children's game.
Search engines.Ask Jeeves: The 1996 site let you type questions in plain English, with a butler mascot named after the valet in P. G. Wodehouse's stories.
Search engines.AltaVista: Launched in 1995 by Digital Equipment, it was one of the first to index much of the web, and Yahoo bought it in 2003.
Search engines.Baidu: China's leading search engine, founded in 2000 and named after a Song-dynasty poem.
Search engines.Yandex: Russia's top search engine began in 1997, and the name stands for yet another indexer.
Search engines.Lycos: Founded in 1994 at Carnegie Mellon, it's named after the wolf spider Lycosidae.
Search engines.Ecosia: A German search engine that uses its ad revenue to plant trees.
Search engines.Chrome: A browser that you use to access search engines, not a search engine itself.
Search engines.Firefox: A browser by Mozilla, not an engine for searching, though it lets you pick one.
Search engines.Safari: A browser, not a search engine, but Google pays Apple billions to be its default search there.
Search engines.Wikipedia: An encyclopedia with its own search box, but not a web search engine.
Search engines.Reddit: A social site whose posts are indexed by search engines, but isn't a search engine.
Search engines.eBay: An auction marketplace that started in 1995, and its first sale was reportedly a broken laser pointer.
Search engines.Twitter: A social network, now called X, and not a search engine, though its search tool is popular.
Search engines.Facebook: A social network, and it's not a search engine, despite its own search bar.
Search engines.Netflix: A streaming service, which has its own search but isn't a general engine.
Search engines.Instagram: A photo-sharing app that Facebook bought in 2012 for about a billion dollars.
Search engines.Spotify: A music streaming service from Sweden, launched in 2008.
Search engines.Gmail: Google's email service, which is not a search engine, even if it searches your mail very well.
Search engines.Edge: Microsoft's web browser, which uses Bing for search but isn't one.
Search engines.Excel: A spreadsheet program with a search tool inside, but not a search engine.

Open-source software.Linux: Linus Torvalds began it in 1991 as a hobby, and it now runs most servers and every Android phone's core.
Open-source software.Firefox: Firefox grew from the code of Netscape's browser and is run by the nonprofit Mozilla.
Open-source software.VLC: VLC plays almost any video file and is made by the French nonprofit VideoLAN, and its traffic-cone icon is famous.
Open-source software.WordPress: WordPress powers a large share of all websites, over a third by some counts.
Open-source software.Python: Python is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake, and it's one of the most popular programming languages.
Open-source software.Blender: Blender is a free 3D tool used in professional films and has been open source since 2002.
Open-source software.GIMP: GIMP stands for GNU Image Manipulation Program and is a free alternative to Photoshop.
Open-source software.LibreOffice: LibreOffice was forked from OpenOffice in 2010 and offers free versions of Word and Excel.
Open-source software.Git: Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005 for Linux development, and it's now the standard way to track code.
Open-source software.Apache: The Apache web server has powered a huge share of websites since the 1990s.
Open-source software.Audacity: Audacity is a free audio editor beloved by podcasters.
Open-source software.Windows: Windows is proprietary Microsoft software whose source code isn't public.
Open-source software.macOS: macOS is built on open-source Darwin but is mostly proprietary Apple software.
Open-source software.Photoshop: Photoshop is Adobe's proprietary image editor, and it's sold by subscription.
Open-source software.Microsoft Word: Word is proprietary and part of Microsoft 365.
Open-source software.Excel: Excel is Microsoft's proprietary spreadsheet program, unlike LibreOffice's Calc.
Open-source software.iOS: iOS is Apple's closed operating system, whereas Android has an open-source base.
Open-source software.Netflix: Netflix is a streaming service that uses open-source tools but is itself a proprietary service.
Open-source software.Spotify: Spotify's apps and service are proprietary, even though the company has published some internal tools as open source.
Open-source software.Final Cut Pro: Final Cut Pro is Apple's proprietary video editor.
Open-source software.AutoCAD: AutoCAD is Autodesk's proprietary design software.
Open-source software.Minecraft: Minecraft's main game is proprietary, although many community mods exist.
Open-source software.Zoom: Zoom is proprietary video conferencing software.
Open-source software.Outlook: Outlook is Microsoft's proprietary email client.

Tech brands named after a person.Dell: Michael Dell started it in 1984 from his University of Texas dorm room, originally under the name PC's Limited.
Tech brands named after a person.Hewlett-Packard: Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard flipped a coin to decide whose name came first, in their famous Palo Alto garage.
Tech brands named after a person.Tesla: Named for inventor Nikola Tesla, whose alternating-current induction motor inspired the company's first car motor.
Tech brands named after a person.Siemens: Founded by Werner von Siemens in 1847 to build telegraph equipment; it grew into an engineering giant.
Tech brands named after a person.Philips: Gerard Philips and his father Frederik founded it in 1891, initially to make light bulbs.
Tech brands named after a person.Bose: Founded in 1964 by MIT professor Amar Bose, who set out to build better audio after being let down by a hi-fi system.
Tech brands named after a person.Ericsson: Lars Magnus Ericsson opened a telegraph repair shop in Stockholm in 1876, and the company grew from there.
Tech brands named after a person.Dyson: James Dyson built over 5,000 prototypes before his bagless vacuum cleaner worked.
Tech brands named after a person.McAfee: The antivirus firm is named for John McAfee, who left decades ago and later became a notorious fugitive.
Tech brands named after a person.Bloomberg: Michael Bloomberg founded it in 1981 after being let go from Salomon Brothers; his Terminal became Wall Street's staple.
Tech brands named after a person.Apple: Steve Jobs reportedly chose the name after visiting an apple farm; no founder was named Apple.
Tech brands named after a person.Google: A misspelling of googol, the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.
Tech brands named after a person.Amazon: Named after the river, partly for its size; Bezos first considered calling it Cadabra.
Tech brands named after a person.Intel: A contraction of Integrated Electronics; the founders' first idea of Moore Noyce was already taken by a hotel chain.
Tech brands named after a person.Microsoft: A blend of microcomputer and software, coined by Bill Gates in a 1975 letter to Paul Allen.
Tech brands named after a person.Sony: Mixes the Latin sonus, meaning sound, with a slangy Japanese term for 'sonny boy'.
Tech brands named after a person.Nokia: It is named after the Finnish town and river where the company's paper mill was set up in the 1860s.
Tech brands named after a person.Samsung: Korean for 'three stars'; founded in 1938, it began as a trading company selling dried fish and groceries.
Tech brands named after a person.Oracle: Named after a CIA project that co-founder Larry Ellison worked on earlier.
Tech brands named after a person.Lenovo: 'Le' comes from Legend, the company's old name, and 'novo' is Latin for new.
Tech brands named after a person.Xerox: From xerography, a word built on Greek roots meaning dry writing.
Tech brands named after a person.Cisco: Short for San Francisco, and the Golden Gate Bridge inspired its logo.
Tech brands named after a person.Adobe: Named after Adobe Creek in Los Altos, California, which ran behind co-founder John Warnock's house.
Tech brands named after a person.Nvidia: From Latin invidia, meaning envy; the founders used 'NV' as a placeholder in file names.

Websites with a .org address.Wikipedia: Run by the nonprofit Wikimedia Foundation, its wikipedia.org holds millions of articles in hundreds of languages.
Websites with a .org address.Mozilla: The maker of Firefox, which grew from the open-sourced Netscape code in 1998.
Websites with a .org address.Craigslist: Craig Newmark started it in 1995 as an email list, and it has stayed a spartan, mostly text site at craigslist.org.
Websites with a .org address.Khan Academy: Sal Khan began with tutoring videos for a cousin, and today it's a nonprofit offering free lessons at khanacademy.org.
Websites with a .org address.Internet Archive: Home of the Wayback Machine, which has saved hundreds of billions of web pages at archive.org.
Websites with a .org address.Signal: The encrypted messenger run by the nonprofit Signal Foundation at signal.org.
Websites with a .org address.NPR: National Public Radio, a nonprofit network founded in 1970, lives at npr.org.
Websites with a .org address.PBS: The Public Broadcasting Service, founded in 1969, uses pbs.org.
Websites with a .org address.Red Cross: The humanitarian movement began after Henri Dunant's account of the 1859 Battle of Solferino; its emblem reverses Switzerland's flag.
Websites with a .org address.Python: The language's official home is python.org, run by a nonprofit foundation.
Websites with a .org address.Project Gutenberg: Founded by Michael Hart in 1971, it is the oldest digital library, with tens of thousands of free books at gutenberg.org.
Websites with a .org address.TED: A trap: it uses ted.com, a .com address despite its nonprofit conference roots.
Websites with a .org address.Duolingo: The green owl language app lives at duolingo.com; it's a for-profit company founded in 2011.
Websites with a .org address.Reddit: Reddit uses reddit.com, and it's a commercial company founded in 2005.
Websites with a .org address.Amazon: No surprise: amazon.com, the site that took Jeff Bezos from books to nearly everything.
Websites with a .org address.YouTube: YouTube is at youtube.com; it launched in 2005 and Google bought it in 2006.
Websites with a .org address.Netflix: Netflix is at netflix.com, and the company began by mailing DVDs in 1998.
Websites with a .org address.IMDb: IMDb uses imdb.com, grew from a 1990 fan-built Usenet database, and is now owned by Amazon.
Websites with a .org address.eBay: eBay uses ebay.com and launched in 1995 as AuctionWeb.
Websites with a .org address.Etsy: Etsy uses etsy.com, a marketplace for handmade goods since 2005.
Websites with a .org address.Quora: Quora uses quora.com, a question-and-answer site founded in 2009.
