Characters in Dracula.Count Dracula: Bram Stoker's 1897 vampire was partly inspired by Transylvanian legend and the name of the historical Vlad the Impaler, whose father was called Dracul.
Characters in Dracula.Jonathan Harker: The young English solicitor travels to Transylvania to sell Dracula a house and quickly realises he's a prisoner.
Characters in Dracula.Mina Harker: Jonathan's clever wife organises the team's notes and typed records, and helps track Dracula by using his hypnotic link to her.
Characters in Dracula.Lucy Westenra: Mina's glamorous friend is bitten by Dracula, dies and returns as a vampire, and becomes the novel's first big horror.
Characters in Dracula.Van Helsing: The Dutch professor and doctor leads the vampire hunters and carries garlic, crucifixes and wooden stakes.
Characters in Dracula.Renfield: The asylum patient who eats flies and spiders in order to gain life force serves as Dracula's willing servant.
Characters in Dracula.Dr. Seward: Lucy's suitor runs the asylum next to Carfax Abbey and records his thoughts on a phonograph, then new technology.
Characters in Dracula.Quincey Morris: The Texan adventurer is one of Lucy's suitors and dies in the final fight, his bowie knife helping kill the Count.
Characters in Dracula.Arthur Holmwood: Lucy's fiancé, later Lord Godalming, is forced to drive a stake through her heart to free her soul.
Characters in Dracula.Victor Frankenstein: Mary Shelley's scientist created his monster in 1818, eighty years before Dracula.
Characters in Dracula.Igor: The hunchbacked lab assistant was a creation of the movies and has nothing to do with Stoker.
Characters in Dracula.Dr. Jekyll: Stevenson's respectable doctor who splits into Mr. Hyde appeared in 1886, so he's a different horror classic.
Characters in Dracula.Mr. Hyde: The evil side of Dr. Jekyll comes from Stevenson's 1886 novella, not Stoker's.
Characters in Dracula.Dorian Gray: Wilde's beautiful young man, whose portrait ages in his place, is a different Gothic tale from 1890.
Characters in Dracula.Carmilla: Sheridan Le Fanu's female vampire came out in 1872, about 25 years before Dracula, and inspired Stoker.
Characters in Dracula.Elizabeth Lavenza: Victor Frankenstein's fiancée is from Shelley's Frankenstein, not Dracula.
Characters in Dracula.Captain Nemo: Verne's submariner has no Gothic horror in his story.
Characters in Dracula.Quasimodo: Hugo's bell-ringer of Notre-Dame is a hunchback, but he is not a monster in the vampire sense.
Characters in Dracula.Esmeralda: The Gypsy dancer of The Hunchback of Notre-Dame belongs to Hugo, not Stoker.
Characters in Dracula.Count Orlok: The vampire of the 1922 film Nosferatu is an unauthorised copy of Dracula, and Stoker's widow sued to have prints destroyed.
Characters in Dracula.Sherlock Holmes: Conan Doyle's detective is a rival Victorian icon, and a vampire hunter only in pastiches.
Characters in Dracula.Lestat: Anne Rice's vampire stars in 1976's Interview with the Vampire, not in Stoker's book.
Characters in Dracula.Edward Cullen: Stephenie Meyer's sparkly teenage vampire in Twilight is a 21st-century creation.
Characters in Dracula.Barnabas Collins: The vampire of the 1960s soap Dark Shadows is a TV invention, not Stoker's.

Things that are usually brown.Chocolate: Chocolate's brown comes from cocoa beans, which are fermented and roasted, and that process also builds its flavour.
Things that are usually brown.Coffee: Coffee turns brown in roasting, when the beans' sugars and amino acids react, called the Maillard reaction.
Things that are usually brown.Acorn: An oak tree can take about 20 years or more before it starts producing acorns.
Things that are usually brown.Cinnamon: Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a tree, and it curls into the familiar quills as it dries.
Things that are usually brown.Peanut butter: Peanuts are not nuts but legumes, and it takes around 540 peanuts to make a 12-ounce jar of peanut butter.
Things that are usually brown.American football: The ball is nicknamed "the pigskin" though it's cowhide, and the brown leather is usually left natural.
Things that are usually brown.Cardboard box: The brown colour is unbleached wood pulp, and most boxes are made of recycled fibre.
Things that are usually brown.Gingerbread man: The gingerbread man's brown comes from molasses and spices, and Queen Elizabeth I reportedly had gingerbread figures made of guests.
Things that are usually brown.Coconut shell: The hairy shell is the coconut's stone, and it is used for charcoal, bowls and bikini tops.
Things that are usually brown.Chestnut: Chestnuts are roasted by street vendors in many cities, and the tree was nearly wiped out in the US by blight.
Things that are usually brown.Pinecone: Pinecones close when wet and open when dry, so they release seeds in dry weather that carries them.
Things that are usually brown.Grizzly bear: Grizzlies are usually brown, with silver-tipped fur that gave them the name "grizzled".
Things that are usually brown.Hazelnut: Hazelnuts are called filberts too, and most of the world's supply grows in Turkey.
Things that are usually brown.Lemon: Lemons are yellow, and the fruit is acidic from citric acid.
Things that are usually brown.Snow: Snow is white, and fresh powder is mostly air.
Things that are usually brown.Fire truck: Fire trucks are mostly red, and the colour is a tradition rather than a rule.
Things that are usually brown.Grass: Grass is green when alive, and goes brown when dormant or dry.
Things that are usually brown.Sky: The sky is blue on clear days, because of how air scatters sunlight.
Things that are usually brown.Banana: A banana is yellow, and it gets brown spots as it ripens.
Things that are usually brown.Pumpkin: Pumpkins are orange and, like squash, grow on vines.
Things that are usually brown.Strawberry: Strawberries are red, and each has around 200 seeds on the outside.
Things that are usually brown.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink, and they eat with their heads upside down.
Things that are usually brown.Milk: Milk is white, though chocolate milk is a brown variation.
Things that are usually brown.Lime: Limes are green, and key limes are smaller and more acidic.

Things that feel rough.Sandpaper: Sandpaper grades run by grit number, and higher means finer: 400 feels almost smooth while 40 is brutally coarse.
Things that feel rough.Tree bark: Bark texture is a field clue to species: oak is deeply furrowed, while birch peels away in thin papery strips.
Things that feel rough.Brick: A brick's gritty face is porous, and a dry one can soak up a surprising amount of water like a sponge.
Things that feel rough.Pumice stone: Pumice is volcanic rock so full of gas bubbles that it floats on water, and it's abrasive enough to scrub rough skin.
Things that feel rough.Nail file: Emery boards are named for emery, a gritty natural mix rich in corundum, the same mineral that forms rubies and sapphires.
Things that feel rough.Cheese grater: The Microplane began as a woodworking rasp until a home cook tried it on lemon zest and it conquered the kitchen.
Things that feel rough.Sharkskin: Shark skin is covered in tiny tooth-like scales called dermal denticles; stroke it tail to head and it rasps like sandpaper.
Things that feel rough.Cat's tongue: A cat's tongue is covered in tiny backward-facing hooks of keratin that work like a comb and a rasp on meat and fur.
Things that feel rough.Burlap sack: Burlap is woven from jute fibers, and its coarse, scratchy weave is why it's used for coffee sacks and sandbags.
Things that feel rough.Steel wool: Steel wool can burn: touch a 9-volt battery to it and the fine strands glow and spark as they oxidize.
Things that feel rough.Coral: Coral skeletons are hard, sharp limestone, and coral cuts are notorious for healing slowly because grit and bacteria get trapped in them.
Things that feel rough.Silk: Silk is smooth because its protein fibers are long and uniform; a single cocoon can unwind into nearly a kilometer of thread.
Things that feel rough.Window glass: Window glass feels smooth because it hardens without crystals; the tale that old panes slowly flow thicker is a myth.
Things that feel rough.Satin: Satin is a weave, not a fiber: long threads float over the surface, giving it that glossy, slippery face.
Things that feel rough.Polished marble: Polishing marble fills microscopic pits so light reflects instead of scattering, turning a dull rock into a mirror-like surface.
Things that feel rough.Ice: Ice is slick thanks to a thin liquid-like layer at its surface, and scientists still argue over exactly why it forms.
Things that feel rough.Pearl: A pearl is smooth because a mollusk coats an irritant in layer after layer of nacre, the same material lining the shell.
Things that feel rough.Balloon: Latex balloons are smooth and stretchy, and a rubbed one can cling to a wall thanks to static electricity.
Things that feel rough.Mirror: A modern mirror is glass with a thin metal coating, usually silver or aluminum, on the back; the glass just protects it.
Things that feel rough.Bowling ball: Bowling balls are polished smooth, but lane conditions and grip needs mean players often have the surface sanded or roughed.
Things that feel rough.Cling film: Cling film clings through static attraction and gentle molecular forces, so it sticks to itself with no glue at all.
Things that feel rough.Rose petal: Rose petals feel velvety thanks to tiny cone-shaped surface cells, which also help water droplets cling to them.
Things that feel rough.Baby's cheek: Infant skin is thinner than adult skin, which is part of why it feels so soft, and it loses moisture faster too.
Things that feel rough.Butter: Butter is roughly 80 percent fat and softens near room temperature, which is why it feels smooth and spreads so easily.

Things that are usually wet.Tongue: The human tongue is covered with thousands of taste buds, and saliva keeps it wet, which is needed for you to taste anything at all.
Things that are usually wet.Eyeball: Your tears and a thin film coat each eye, and blinking spreads them, as a dry cornea would damage your vision quickly.
Things that are usually wet.Ocean: Oceans cover about 71 percent of Earth and hold roughly 97 percent of its water, though most of the deep sea is unexplored.
Things that are usually wet.Swimming pool: A standard Olympic pool holds about 2.5 million liters of water, enough to fill many thousands of bathtubs.
Things that are usually wet.Dog's nose: A dog's nose is wet because moisture traps scent particles, and dogs also lick it to sample smells.
Things that are usually wet.Waterfall: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops about 979 meters, nearly a kilometer, and much of its water turns to mist before it reaches the base.
Things that are usually wet.Raindrop: Raindrops aren't teardrop-shaped as drawn; small ones are round and larger ones flatten into a shape like a hamburger bun.
Things that are usually wet.Frog's skin: Many frogs absorb water and even breathe partly through their moist skin, and they dry out and die if it can't stay damp.
Things that are usually wet.Puddle: Puddles are shallow pools left by rain, and the smell after rain, petrichor, comes from soil compounds released by drops.
Things that are usually wet.Slug: Slugs are about 90 percent water and leave a slime trail, and they avoid dry air because they dehydrate fast.
Things that are usually wet.Desert sand: Desert sand is famously dry, but under the surface dunes can hold surprising moisture, and it rarely rains for months.
Things that are usually wet.Cracker: Crackers are crisp because they contain very little water, which is why they go stale and soggy if left open in humid air.
Things that are usually wet.Chalk: Chalk is a soft limestone made of tiny fossil sea plankton shells, and blackboard chalk is now usually gypsum.
Things that are usually wet.Paper: Paper begins as pulp in lots of water, but it's dried and pressed, and it weakens when wet again.
Things that are usually wet.Feather: Feathers are coated in oil from the bird's preen gland, which helps water bead and roll off a duck's back.
Things that are usually wet.Saltine: The saltine is also called a soda cracker, and it's baked until very dry, so a cup of soup will soften it quickly.
Things that are usually wet.Cotton ball: Cotton is highly absorbent and can soak up many times its weight in water, but it's dry until used.
Things that are usually wet.Toast: Toasting dries bread out and browns it through the Maillard reaction, and the result is a crisp, dry slice.
Things that are usually wet.Dry cereal: Cereal is built to stay crunchy in the box, and milk is exactly what turns it soggy, which is why the flakes get a sugar coating.
Things that are usually wet.Flour: Flour is dry powder that's explosive in suspended dust, as flour mills have exploded when dust ignited.
Things that are usually wet.Sand dune: Dunes migrate slowly as wind carries grains up the windward side, and some singing dunes hum when sand avalanches.
Things that are usually wet.Cactus spine: Cactus spines are modified leaves that reduce water loss, and they also shade the plant and funnel dew into the plant.
Things that are usually wet.Potato chip: The potato chip was reportedly invented in 1853 by chef George Crum at a New York restaurant, and it fries until most of the water is gone.
Things that are usually wet.Rice cake: Rice cakes are made by puffing rice grains with heat and pressure, and the result is dry and crisp.

Major London railway terminals.Paddington: Designed by Brunel and opened in 1854, it's the London terminus for the Great Western Railway, and a bronze statue of the bear stands on the concourse.
Major London railway terminals.Waterloo: London's busiest station, named after Napoleon's defeat in 1815, has the Victory Arch and a famously large clock above the main concourse.
Major London railway terminals.Euston: The first intercity railway terminus in London, opened in 1837, and trains from it head to northwest England and Scotland.
Major London railway terminals.King's Cross: The station with a Harry Potter platform marker was built in 1852, and its modern concourse features a lovely lattice roof.
Major London railway terminals.Victoria: Opened in 1860, this southern London terminal serves Gatwick Express trains, and sits near Buckingham Palace.
Major London railway terminals.Liverpool Street: A big station in the City of London, built over a former Bedlam asylum burial ground, serving Stansted Airport and East Anglia.
Major London railway terminals.Marylebone: The smallest and last of London's great Victorian terminals, opened in 1899, and quiet enough that it was once threatened with closure.
Major London railway terminals.St Pancras: Its Gothic Revival hotel frontage looks like a cathedral, and today it hosts Eurostar trains to Paris and Brussels.
Major London railway terminals.Charing Cross: The station stands near the spot used as the official center of London, from which road distances to the capital are measured.
Major London railway terminals.London Bridge: One of the oldest railway stations in the world, opened in 1836, and a major hub rebuilt around the Shard skyscraper.
Major London railway terminals.Fenchurch Street: A compact City terminal serving Essex, and unusual for its small size, with just four platforms, and it's one of London's least-used major stations.
Major London railway terminals.Grand Central: A New York terminal, not London. It has 44 platforms, the most of any station in the world, plus a famous celestial ceiling.
Major London railway terminals.Penn Station: New York's busiest rail hub, and a trap here because it's American, but it has been rebuilt around its tunnels since 1910.
Major London railway terminals.Gare du Nord: Paris's busiest station, Europe's busiest too, and the Eurostar terminal there connects it to London St Pancras.
Major London railway terminals.Gare de Lyon: A Paris station with an ornate clock tower and Le Train Bleu, a lavish restaurant with gilded ceilings, but it's not in London.
Major London railway terminals.Union Station: The name of grand stations in Washington, Chicago, Toronto and more, but not London, so it doesn't fit.
Major London railway terminals.Shinjuku: Tokyo's mega station with more than 200 exits, and it's one of the busiest in the world, but nowhere near London.
Major London railway terminals.Waverley: Edinburgh's main station, named after Walter Scott's novels, and it's the only major station in the world named after a book series.
Major London railway terminals.New Street: Birmingham's main station, a trap since it's not in London, was rebuilt in 2015 with a shiny stainless-steel exterior.
Major London railway terminals.Lime Street: Liverpool's grand station, opened in 1836, one of the world's oldest mainline terminals, and nothing to do with London.
Major London railway terminals.Temple Meads: Bristol's station, designed by Brunel, with a Tudor-style frontage, and it's not in London.
Major London railway terminals.Wembley: Famous for its stadium, not for being one of London's great terminals, though Wembley does have local stations.
Major London railway terminals.Big Ben: The name actually refers to the great bell, not the clock tower, which is called Elizabeth Tower, and it's no railway terminal.
Major London railway terminals.Termini: Rome's main railway station, the largest in Italy, named after the nearby Baths of Diocletian, not in London.

Things on a farm.Barn: Barns' large doors and haylofts were designed for storing hay, and some barn raisings once involved a whole community in a single day.
Things on a farm.Tractor: Early steam traction engines of the 1800s led to the gasoline tractor in 1892, built by John Froelich in Iowa.
Things on a farm.Silo: The word comes from Greek for a pit to store grain, and silage ferments inside, which smells quite pungent.
Things on a farm.Haystack: Hay is dried grass, and farmers once built stacks with thatched tops to shed rain until the baler arrived.
Things on a farm.Scarecrow: Scarecrows date back at least to ancient Egypt, and many clever crows learn to ignore them after a few days.
Things on a farm.Pigsty: Pigs are clean animals when given room, and they roll in mud mainly to cool off because they can't sweat.
Things on a farm.Chicken coop: Hens lay best with about 14 hours of light, so farmers often add lights in winter to keep eggs coming.
Things on a farm.Combine harvester: The machine combines reaping, threshing and winnowing in one pass, and one modern machine can harvest tons of wheat per hour.
Things on a farm.Stable: Horses sleep both standing and lying down, and they can doze on their feet thanks to a locking mechanism in their legs.
Things on a farm.Trough: Animals drink or eat from it, and the word comes from an Old English word meaning a tree or wooden vessel.
Things on a farm.Plow: The plow is one of agriculture's oldest tools, and early versions were pulled by oxen over 5,000 years ago.
Things on a farm.Paddock: A small field kept for horses, and the word comes from Old English 'pearroc', meaning a fenced area.
Things on a farm.Orchard: Trees in an orchard, and most apple trees need pollen from a different variety to produce fruit.
Things on a farm.Escalator: A moving staircase that belongs in malls and stations, not in the fields.
Things on a farm.Turnstile: A rotating gate for crowds at stadiums and transit, and the farm may have a gate but not a turnstile.
Things on a farm.Parking meter: Invented in 1935 in Oklahoma City, it's a city feature, and out in the country you rarely need one.
Things on a farm.Skyscraper: Called a skyscraper since the late 1800s, and the first was the 1885 Home Insurance Building in Chicago.
Things on a farm.Subway: An underground railway of cities, and no farm has one, though some barns sit on subway-sized root cellars.
Things on a farm.Lighthouse: Coastal beacons, and the oldest known was the ancient Pharos of Alexandria, but farms rarely need one.
Things on a farm.Runway: Airport strips and fashion catwalks both use the word, but a farm rarely does, except crop-dusters using a field strip.
Things on a farm.Taxi rank: A line of waiting cabs in a city, a thing that doesn't fit on a farm.
Things on a farm.Traffic light: The first electric one was installed in Cleveland in 1914, and rural farms rarely need one.
Things on a farm.Roller coaster: A thrill ride from amusement parks, though some farms offer pumpkin patches and corn mazes in autumn.
Things on a farm.Jet bridge: The enclosed walkway between terminal and plane, belonging to airports, and nowhere near a farmyard.

Hindu festivals.Diwali: Diwali, the festival of lights, marks the triumph of light over darkness. Families light oil lamps called diyas, and it is also marked by Sikhs and Jains.
Hindu festivals.Holi: Holi, the festival of colors, welcomes spring with people throwing colored powder and water. It also recalls the story of Prahlada and Holika.
Hindu festivals.Navratri: Navratri means 'nine nights', honoring the goddess Durga. In Gujarat it is celebrated with energetic garba dances.
Hindu festivals.Dussehra: Dussehra celebrates the victory of Rama over the demon king Ravana. Giant effigies of Ravana are burned across India.
Hindu festivals.Raksha Bandhan: On this day sisters tie a protective thread, a rakhi, on brothers' wrists, and brothers promise to protect them.
Hindu festivals.Ganesh Chaturthi: This festival honors elephant-headed Ganesha. Huge clay idols are paraded and then immersed in water, especially in Mumbai.
Hindu festivals.Janmashtami: Janmashtami celebrates Krishna's birth, and devotees often fast until midnight. In Maharashtra, human pyramids break a pot of curd.
Hindu festivals.Pongal: Pongal is a South Indian harvest festival named after a dish of rice cooked in milk until it overflows, symbolizing abundance.
Hindu festivals.Onam: Onam is Kerala's harvest festival, with a huge feast on banana leaves, flower carpets, and snake boat races.
Hindu festivals.Makar Sankranti: Makar Sankranti marks the sun's move into Capricorn, and is one of the few Hindu festivals on a fixed solar date, in mid-January. Kite flying is popular.
Hindu festivals.Durga Puja: Durga Puja is especially big in Bengal, with elaborate temporary pavilions called pandals. UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2021.
Hindu festivals.Eid al-Adha: Eid al-Adha is the Muslim feast of sacrifice remembering Ibrahim, celebrated with prayers and shared meat. Not Hindu.
Hindu festivals.Vesak: Vesak is a Buddhist festival, with lanterns and charity, marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death.
Hindu festivals.Hanukkah: Hanukkah is the Jewish festival of lights, which can seem like Diwali, but it belongs to a different faith.
Hindu festivals.Ramadan: Ramadan is the Muslim fasting month, shifting about ten days earlier each year because the calendar is lunar.
Hindu festivals.Purim: Purim is a Jewish celebration of the rescue told in the Book of Esther, with costumes and noisemakers.
Hindu festivals.Songkran: Songkran is the Thai New Year in April, famed for water fights that started as a gentle blessing ritual.
Hindu festivals.Obon: Obon is a Japanese Buddhist festival honoring ancestors, with dances and lanterns floating on rivers.
Hindu festivals.Nowruz: Nowruz, the Persian new year on the spring equinox, goes back over 3,000 years in Zoroastrian tradition.
Hindu festivals.Easter: Easter celebrates the resurrection in the Christian tradition. It is not among the Hindu festivals.
Hindu festivals.Chuseok: Chuseok is Korea's harvest festival in autumn, with rice cakes called songpyeon and honoring of ancestors.
Hindu festivals.Tet: Tet is the Vietnamese lunar new year, Vietnam's biggest holiday. The family gatherings are similar to Hindu festivals, but it is a different tradition.
Hindu festivals.Passover: Passover is a Jewish festival remembering the Exodus from Egypt, with a seder meal and matzah, not a Hindu one.
Hindu festivals.Lent: Lent is the forty-day Christian season of fasting before Easter, so it isn't a Hindu festival.

Watch brands.Rolex: Rolex's Oyster case, launched in 1926, was the first truly waterproof wristwatch, and the brand's crown logo is familiar worldwide.
Watch brands.Omega: Omega is the watch worn on the Moon: the Speedmaster was the one chosen by NASA, and it went along on Apollo 11.
Watch brands.Tag Heuer: TAG stands for Techniques d'Avant Garde, added after buying Heuer in 1985; Heuer's stopwatches had timed Olympic events for decades.
Watch brands.Swatch: This Swiss brand's 1983 plastic watches saved the Swiss watch industry, and its name is a blend of second watch.
Watch brands.Casio: Casio's G-Shock, launched in 1983, was designed by an engineer who dropped his watch and vowed to build one that could survive anything.
Watch brands.Seiko: In 1969 this Japanese company launched the Astron, the world's first quartz wristwatch, which shook up the Swiss industry.
Watch brands.Patek Philippe: Founded in Geneva in 1839, the Swiss maker has a slogan about the next generation, and made some of the priciest watches ever auctioned.
Watch brands.Cartier: Louis Cartier designed one of the first modern wristwatches, the Santos, in 1904 for aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont.
Watch brands.Breitling: Based in Switzerland, it is closely associated with aviation, and its chronographs were made for pilots.
Watch brands.Tissot: Founded in 1853 in Le Locle, Switzerland, it is a major watch brand and the official timekeeper of many sports.
Watch brands.Timex: This American brand's old advertising line was that it takes a licking and keeps on ticking.
Watch brands.Citizen: Citizen is Japanese and made the first solar-powered watch, and has its roots in Tokyo.
Watch brands.Audemars Piguet: The Royal Oak, an octagonal luxury sports watch designed by Gérald Genta in 1972, made this Swiss maker's name.
Watch brands.Ray-Ban: Ray-Ban makes sunglasses; its Aviators were first produced for US pilots in the 1930s.
Watch brands.Oakley: Oakley is American eyewear, founded by Jim Jannard, and not a watchmaker.
Watch brands.Louboutin: Christian Louboutin is a French shoe designer, and his shoes famously have red soles.
Watch brands.Manolo Blahnik: Manolo Blahnik is a Spanish-born shoe designer whose name Sex and the City made famous.
Watch brands.Birkenstock: Birkenstock is a German sandal brand with a cork footbed, and not watches.
Watch brands.Crocs: Crocs are foam clogs, and no watchmakers, although you can wear charms on them.
Watch brands.Levi's: Levi's is a denim maker, and not a watch brand.
Watch brands.Converse: Converse's Chuck Taylor sneakers are named after a basketball player and are among history's best-selling shoes.
Watch brands.Kodak: Kodak invented the first digital camera in 1975, and it sells cameras and film rather than watches.
Watch brands.Nikon: Nikon is a Japanese camera maker, and not watches.
Watch brands.Zara: Zara is a Spanish clothing chain, not a watchmaker.

Annual events held in the UK.Glastonbury: Held on a Somerset dairy farm since 1970, it is the world's largest greenfield music festival, and the farm's cows share the site.
Annual events held in the UK.Wimbledon: The oldest tennis tournament in the world, since 1877, it keeps its grass courts, white dress code, and strawberries and cream.
Annual events held in the UK.Edinburgh Fringe: It is the world's largest arts festival, and it grew from eight companies who turned up uninvited to the 1947 Edinburgh International Festival.
Annual events held in the UK.Hogmanay: Scotland's New Year celebration is a major party, and its Edinburgh street party draws tens of thousands.
Annual events held in the UK.Bonfire Night: Every 5 November, the UK burns effigies of Guy Fawkes and sets off fireworks, to recall the 1605 Gunpowder Plot.
Annual events held in the UK.Reading Festival: One of the world's oldest music festivals, it began as a jazz and blues event in 1961 and now has twin sites.
Annual events held in the UK.Burns Night: Held on 25 January for the poet Robert Burns, it features haggis, whisky and the poem Address to a Haggis.
Annual events held in the UK.Chelsea Flower Show: The Royal Horticultural Society's show runs in London each May, and the Queen was a regular visitor.
Annual events held in the UK.Hay Festival: The Welsh town of Hay-on-Wye, famed for its second-hand bookshops, hosts a literary festival that Bill Clinton called the Woodstock of the mind.
Annual events held in the UK.Download Festival: This metal festival is held at Donington Park, where it began in 2003, and the home of motor racing.
Annual events held in the UK.Coachella: Coachella is in California, but plenty of the British festival circuit is a long way off, so this one is not in the UK.
Annual events held in the UK.Burning Man: Burning Man in Nevada's desert ends by burning a huge wooden figure, which is a long way from Britain.
Annual events held in the UK.Kentucky Derby: The Kentucky Derby takes place in Louisville, where winners get a blanket of roses, and it is not British.
Annual events held in the UK.Cannes Film Festival: Cannes holds its film festival on the French Riviera and awards the Palme d'Or, so it is not a UK event.
Annual events held in the UK.La Tomatina: La Tomatina is a tomato food fight with about 120 tonnes of fruit in the Spanish town of Buñol.
Annual events held in the UK.Running of the Bulls: Pamplona's bull run is part of San Fermín and draws thousands of runners to Spain every July.
Annual events held in the UK.Rio Carnival: Rio's Carnival is Brazil's pre-Lent spectacle, and its samba parades are held in a special stadium called the Sambadrome.
Annual events held in the UK.Lollapalooza: Founded by Perry Farrell in 1991 as a touring festival, Lollapalooza now sets up in Chicago, not Britain.
Annual events held in the UK.Venice Carnival: Venice's Carnival is known for its elaborate masks, a tradition going back centuries, and it is in Italy.
Annual events held in the UK.Tour de France: The Tour de France takes about three weeks every July and ends on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, so it is French.
Annual events held in the UK.Sundance: Sundance in Utah is named after the Sundance Kid, a Robert Redford role, and is American.
Annual events held in the UK.SXSW: Held in Austin, Texas, SXSW began in 1987 as a music event and expanded to film and tech.
Annual events held in the UK.Tomorrowland: Tomorrowland, held in Boom, Belgium, is among the biggest electronic music festivals in the world.
Annual events held in the UK.Roskilde: Roskilde in Denmark began in 1971 and gives its profits to charity, so it is not British.

Undead creatures.Zombie: The word comes from Haitian vodou. Night of the Living Dead (1968) never uses the word "zombie," calling them ghouls.
Undead creatures.Vampire: The word spread through 1700s European reports of Eastern European corpses supposedly rising to drink blood.
Undead creatures.Mummy: The cursed-mummy movie began with Boris Karloff in 1932. Real mummies were just preserved bodies.
Undead creatures.Lich: A sorcerer who made himself undead by sealing his soul in a phylactery. Dungeons and Dragons popularized them.
Undead creatures.Draugr: A Norse undead guardian of burial mounds in the sagas, with superhuman strength. They became famous in Skyrim.
Undead creatures.Revenant: French for "one who returns." In folklore it's a corpse that rises to haunt the living, which is why it counts as undead.
Undead creatures.Ghost: The spirit of someone dead lingering in the world. Many fantasy lists count it as undead, since it's dead but present.
Undead creatures.Wight: In Tolkien, barrow-wights are evil spirits in burial mounds. Game of Thrones' wights are reanimated corpses.
Undead creatures.Jiangshi: The Chinese hopping corpse, stiff with rigor mortis. Sticky rice and mirrors are said to repel it.
Undead creatures.Dracula: Bram Stoker's 1897 Count, with the name possibly borrowed from the historical Vlad Dracula.
Undead creatures.Werewolf: A living human who transforms, not a dead one. The silver bullet weakness comes mostly from movies.
Undead creatures.Golem: A clay figure animated by magic in Jewish folklore. It was never alive in the first place, so it isn't undead.
Undead creatures.Gargoyle: Stone carvings that guard buildings and drain rainwater. In most stories they're never alive, so never undead.
Undead creatures.Troll: Scandinavian monsters that, in some tales, turn to stone in sunlight. They're alive, not undead.
Undead creatures.Orc: Tolkien's brutish soldiers are a living race, bred by dark powers, and they're mortal.
Undead creatures.Ogre: Man-eating giants of folklore, popularized in French fairy tales. They are living creatures, not dead ones.
Undead creatures.Yeti: A living ape-like creature said to roam the Himalayas. Never dead, so it doesn't fit.
Undead creatures.Siren: The Greek bird-women who lured sailors with song. In Homer they were living monsters, not the dead.
Undead creatures.Centaur: A living half-horse, half-man of Greek myth. Chiron the centaur taught heroes, and he was never dead.
Undead creatures.Leprechaun: Ireland's fairy cobbler is a living trickster guarding gold. The name may derive from a word for "small body."
Undead creatures.Kraken: A Norse sea monster, alive and enormous, said to drag whole ships under. Not undead.
Undead creatures.Minotaur: The half-man, half-bull of Crete, trapped in the Labyrinth by King Minos until Theseus killed him. Alive, not undead.
Undead creatures.Dryad: A tree nymph. The name derives from the Greek word for oak, and she's alive until her tree dies.
Undead creatures.Cyclops: A one-eyed giant such as Polyphemus in the Odyssey. The name means "round-eye," and he's very much alive.
